key_insight: Combine human video imitation for post-grasp motion with a simulation-based filter and a modular policy that separately handles grasping and after-grasp behaviors, enabling robots with non-human hands to learn prehensile tasks from human videos.
problem_solved: Bridges the gap between abundant human video data (good for post-grasp motions) and robot-specific grasping requirements, addressing how to learn complete prehensile manipulation (grasp + post-grasp) when human demonstrations may be infeasible for robot morphologies.
method: Modular policy decomposition: separate grasping module (robot-feasible) and post-grasp skill module (learned from human videos).
Simulation-filtering: use a physics simulator to evaluate and filter human-derived candidate grasps/trajectories to keep only those feasible for the target robot.
Joint training/assembly: train modules with filtered demonstrations and sim-to-real adaptation so the composed policy performs end-to-end prehensile tasks on the robot.
impact: Enables scalable use of large human video datasets to teach robotic manipulation while ensuring robot feasibility, reducing reliance on costly robot demonstrations and improving sample efficiency for real-world deployment.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: human video → extract post-grasp motion → simulation filter → grasp module + post-grasp module → robot execution

paper_title: Imitating What Works: Simulation-Filtered Modular Policy Learning from Human Videos
paper_authors: Albert J. Zhai, Kuo-Hao Zeng, Jiasen Lu, Ali Farhadi, Shenlong Wang
